blocks.en: An interactive software that integrates real-time field sensing, bioreactor monitoring, and automated control to make ReLEAF accessible to farmers.
blocks.text: An interactive software that integrates real-time field sensing, bioreactor monitoring, and automated control to make ReLEAF accessible to farmers.

blocks.en: To make ReLEAF easier to monitor and operate, we developed a digital twin that connects field sensors, bioreactor measurements, and automated controls in one interface. The system tracks crop conditions alongside bioreactor data, including optical density, pH, pressure, and flow, allowing users to monitor both plant health and production status. By integrating real-time measurements with predictive monitoring, the platform helps farmers receive early warnings, track system performance, and manage ReLEAF without specialized biomanufacturing knowledge.

blocks.en: ReLEAF's bioreactor is built to stand beside a rice field and run for weeks, looked after by a rice grower with no laboratory training. The software therefore has five jobs: show what the culture is doing, raise an alarm when a reading or the culture drifts, predict the biomass a few hours ahead, judge from the weather forecast and the crop whether the protectant will be ready when it is needed, and give the answer in plain language. Live readings cover only the first job. The others need the batch simulated ahead of the vessel and the result returned to it. That return is what separates a digital twin from a digital model, which is updated by hand, and a digital shadow, which receives live data but needs a person to act on it [1, 2].

The software therefore has five jobs: show what the culture is doing, raise an alarm when a reading or the culture drifts, predict the biomass a few hours ahead, judge from the weather forecast and the crop whether the protectant will be ready when it is needed, and give the answer in plain language. Live readings cover only the first job. The others need the batch simulated ahead of the vessel and the result returned to it. blocks.en: ReLEAF is an AIoT system: the bioreactor's sensors and valves are wired to a board that logs every reading, a sensor beside the crop reads leaf temperature and leaf wetness, and models learn from those readings. An autoencoder trained on the healthy first 120 hours of the 434-hour run flagged a failing photometer 26.7 hours before its reading became unusable (R2). The amount of protectant cannot be read in-line; it comes from samples drawn by hand and assayed by ELISA and DNPH (section 4). So far the models have run on recorded data after each run and a person makes every decision; the next Digital Twin joins them to the live loop.

blocks.en: Leaf wetness and the rice blast rule
blocks.text: Leaf wetness and the rice blast rule

blocks.en: Leaf wetness is not itself a stress for rice. It matters because blast fungus needs a wet leaf to infect, and infection depends on how long the leaf stays wet and how warm it is, so one sensor reads both channels. The twin applies the BLASTAM rule for leaf blast [3], which counts a wet period as an infection condition when the leaf stays wet for at least 10 hours at a mean of 22 to 25 °C, asks for longer as it gets cooler, and allows no infection below 15 °C or above 25 °C [4]; a dry hour ends the period. Hours already past come from the sensor, and hours ahead are estimated from the forecast, counted as wet when relative humidity reaches 90% [5]. When a period meets the rule, the interface tells the grower to look for lesions five to ten days later.

blocks.en: The sensor has only been on a bench (R3) and its wet threshold is a default. The rule has not been checked against Taiwanese disease records, and a met condition means only that the weather allowed infection. ACC deaminase has not been tested against blast, so blast risk is shown to the grower but does not switch the green light.

blocks.en: Run 7 is the longest clean run: 77 hours in one file, OD to 3.34, no window lost to low signal. Two changes made it possible. Run 5's reading broke down after ten hours, with bubbles in a sixth of its windows and the reference drifting 4.8-fold, so run 6 halved the permeate flow to 12 mL/min and added an acceptance gate that holds the last good value when a window fails its checks. Run 6 then read cleanly to 2.71 at 37 h before its sample beam was lost; run 7 passed that point at 44 h and kept reading.

blocks.en: Fouling stayed far from a cleaning point: the extra pressure across the membrane rose from 2.0 to 3.8 kPa over run 6 and from 1.9 to 4.4 kPa over run 7, as permeability halved from 2520 to 1210 LMH/bar. Each short spike in that trace coincides with zero permeate pressure, which is the permeate side being opened. On run 7 the pH loop logged 53 base doses against a 7.00 target, yet pH still ranged from 6.34 to 7.97.

blocks.en: The twin times induction from both ends. From the field, the forecast and the crop-stress rule give the hour the crop comes under stress, and the light must come on earlier by the time protectant takes to make. From the vessel, the prior sets a target time at hour zero, the Kalman filter updates it, the sensor alarm decides which readings to trust, and the fouling trace shows whether the membrane will still pass permeate. If the culture is ready in time, the twin names the hour to induce; if not, it warns days ahead that the batch cannot meet the demand.

blocks.en: The assays cannot yet set how long to induce. The ELISA figure is flat from hour 1 to hour 41, as expected for a constitutive strain without light; both assays are single samples, and the activity reading is below the quantitation limit with its two readouts 22-fold apart. A person still decides the induction length until the assays are repeated on an induced batch and green light is fitted to the bioreactor.

blocks.en: The next version brings leaf wetness and the weather forecast into the green-light decision. Its seven tabs are what to do now, a live dashboard, growth against its forecast band, weather and blast risk, the batch record, Ask, and setup. It stores every run, so its predictions improve as runs accumulate.

blocks.en: In the Ask tab a farmer pastes their own AI provider’s API key (Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini) and asks about the screen in plain language, for example why the green light is still off. The assistant sees the readings, warnings and advice on screen; it can explain them but cannot move a valve or the light. The key is not saved. On the iGEM wiki the chat is off, because the wiki allows no outside requests.

attrs.en: Digital Twin. A laptop screen showing the twin's dark dashboard, with live growth traces and pump readouts.
Summary
Where the twin's data come from

Seven panels of OD600 against time: run 1 and run 2 hand-sampled against a shake flask, run 3 over 434 hours in-line, run 4 in two logged parts with a 10-hour unlogged gap, run 5 breaking down after ten hours, run 6 rising cleanly over 42 hours with a fitted growth rate, and run 7 across the full width, rising over 77 hours to an optical density of 3.3 with the reading intact.
Results
R1 Photometer calibration
In-line photometer and BioDrop readings against cumulative TiO2 dose from 2 to 60 mg, each with a fitted straight line and its R squared.
A student in a lab coat adds TiO2 suspension by syringe to a stirred bottle of white liquid that is pumped through the black in-line photometer on the desk, while an instructor watches from the side.
Both in-line photometer builds and the BioDrop against cumulative SiO2 dose from 2.5 to 100 mg, each with a fitted straight line and its R squared.
A student in a lab coat pipettes a sample into a cuvette beside the black in-line photometer and its stirred beaker, while an instructor logs the readings on a laptop.
R2 434-hour run
OD600 and the photometer reference channel over the 434-hour batch, with the process event and instrument event shaded and the sensor alarm marked.
R3 Field sensors
The bench rig on a desk: a breadboard carrying the SHT31, an ESP32 on its expansion board, a red RS485 converter, and the white disc of the leaf sensor on its cable, with the logging laptop behind.

Wiring diagram: the ESP32 drives a TTL to RS485 converter on GPIO17 and GPIO16, which carries A and B to the leaf sensor, while the SHT31 sits on the I2C pins GPIO21 and GPIO22. Sensor power is taken from 5 V or a 12 V adapter depending on the spec card.

Leaf minus air temperature for nine bench runs. The incubator sits near plus 1.8 degrees and the stairwell near plus 1.3; the room starts below zero and climbs past plus 1 across its three runs. A side panel gives the mean of each run against its site mean.
R4 Module pressure drop
Pressure drop against flow, with the module fitted and with a jumper only, each fitted through the origin, and the net-module difference curve.
R5 Batch forecasting
Hourly medians of in-line OD600 across the 102-hour run, with a straight line and an exponential fitted to them and the two operator interventions marked.
R6 Light plate
Logistic growth fit to the 19 September LPA run, with the six light arms and the pooled curve.
The light-programmable array running inside an incubator: a white block of capped culture tubes glowing green and red from the LEDs beneath, mounted on a black base on a shaker.
The two digital twins

The bioreactor inside an incubator with its door open: a stirred bottle of amber culture, tubing, the black in-line photometer and wiring, with a peristaltic pump and a laptop showing the dashboard on top.
A laptop screen showing the Digital Twin dashboard: the optical density and pH charts, the four pressure traces, the membrane filtration warnings and the pump and feed valve controls.
The System map tab of the next Digital Twin: a flow diagram of the reservoir, pumps, pinch valve and hollow-fibre module with live pressure, pH, flow and optical density readings on demo data.
The Ask tab of the next Digital Twin: a chat box with example questions on the left, and on the right a panel to choose an AI provider and model and paste an API key.
